title: Flushing: A Charter Before a Native Land Agreement
summary: In present-day northern Queens, Dutch director Willem Kieft authorized Flushing’s settlers in 1645. A later agreement between named Native proprietors and town agents addressed occupied land under English rule while preserving Native gathering rights.
address_label: Approximate historical landscape — not a visitor entrance

why_this_matters: Colonial grants and Native land agreements were different acts. Their sequence shows how settlement expanded, while reserved rights and continuing communities challenge a story of simple disappearance.

history_title: How control of the land changed
history_content:
Flushing in today’s Queens

This is the historic town of Flushing in northern Queens, New York City, a larger district than today’s downtown neighborhood. Its early charter came from the Dutch colony of New Netherland. By the time of the 1684 agreement, England governed the colony as New York. The town’s settlers, the colonial government and the Native landowners were different parties with different interests.

Two different kinds of document

Flushing's land history cannot be reduced to its founding charter. In October 1645, Willem Kieft, director of the Dutch colony of New Netherland, issued a charter authorizing settlers to establish Flushing. Almost forty years later, an agreement with Native proprietors still had to address the land they occupied. The gap between those documents matters: a colonial government claiming power to grant land was not the same thing as Native owners agreeing to a transfer. History of the Town of Flushing

What the charter claimed

The charter authorized settlement, inheritance and development, naming waterways and neighboring colonial grants as boundaries. Its original wording reached toward Long Island's southern shore, but a memorandum added before the charter was sealed limited the southern extent to the hills. That change prevents a modern map from treating the unrevised language as a grant all the way across the island. The charter made provision for settlers' government and resource use; it was issued by Kieft and did not bear the signatures of Native landowners. History of the Town of Flushing

The 1684 agreement

The surviving April 14, 1684 instrument bears Native marks and seals. Waller’s transcription identifies Sackapowsha and other Native proprietors dealing with agents of Flushing’s freeholders: Elias Doughty, Thomas Willett, John Bowne, Matthyas Harvey, Thomas Hickes, Richard Cornell, John Hinchman, Jonathan Wright and Samuel Hoyt. The agents represented the town’s landholding settlers. The surviving instrument records payment and acknowledges nearly forty years of settler occupation without the earlier deed described as missing in the agreement. Waller, pp. 78–79 The document therefore shows a later attempt to establish title over an already settled landscape. Its formal declaration of voluntary agreement is the instrument's wording, not independent evidence about every participant's choices. Flushing Indian deed, April 14, 1684

A right reserved for future generations

The agreement reserved the ability of the Native parties and their heirs to cut bulrushes anywhere within the tract perpetually. This surviving provision matters because it contradicts a simple story of complete departure at the moment of sale. The record links land transfer to an ongoing Native right to gather a useful wetland resource. A history of the deed should explain both the expanding settler claim and the right that the document preserved. Flushing, Past and Present

Descendants continue to tell this history

Native history here continues through people, families and public cultural work. In 2018, Flushing Town Hall announced a program with Matinecock descendants, including artist and cultural educator Tecumseh Ceaser, author and family historian Donna Gentle Spirit Barron, and Chief Reggie Dances With Medicine Ceaser. The program addressed history, cultural protocols and relationships with local institutions. Its organizers explicitly recognized Matinecock people living in Little Neck, elsewhere in Queens and on Long Island. Colonial land records belong beside those continuing community voices, not in place of them. Honoring the First People of Queens

Continue with Matinecock Ancestral Land and Matinecock Way.
whereintheworld_content:
This is a regional reading area for Flushing and northeastern Queens, including Whitestone, Bayside and Little Neck. H. F. Walling’s 1859 town geography supplies the inland setting; modern Queens shorelines and the present county edge orient the coastal margin. These modern edges do not establish the extent of the 1645 charter or the 1684 Native agreement. The historical map alignment differs by up to about 500 metres. Shoreline changes and later boundaries add uncertainty, and the area is not a survey of one land sale or evidence that Native rights ended. The 1645 charter’s restriction to the hills before sealing, rather than its superseded oceanward wording, remains essential to understanding the colonial claim.

Walling’s 1859 map; Modern Queens coastline

The northern reading area includes today's College Point and Tallman Island waterfront. A city assessment describes fill linking parts of Tallman Island to the mainland by the 1920s and later construction on the island. Today's connected shoreline therefore cannot be read as the boundary of the 1645 charter or the 1684 Native agreement. This is modern geographic context for those histories, not a claim that every part of College Point was made by filling water or that Native rights ended at this line.
